content: The sensitivity of the diagnostic tests ranged from 79% to 98%, with overlapping confidence intervals (CIs) in most studies, except for one study that reported a sensitivity of 40%. This particular study enrolled outpatients who were on antiretroviral therapy (ART), which may explain the observed variability. Despite this, no downgrading was applied for inconsistency. One level of downgrading was applied for serious imprecision. The confidence intervals around true positives and false negatives were wide enough to potentially lead to different clinical decisions, depending on the assumed credible limits. Specificity estimates in four studies involving outpatients not on ART ranged from 44% to 63%, with non-overlapping confidence intervals. This variability could not be explained. Additionally, one study involving inpatients reported a specificity of 12%, while another study involving outpatients on ART reported a specificity of 79%. One level of downgrading was applied for serious inconsistency. Another level of downgrading was applied for imprecision due to the wide confidence intervals around true negatives and false positives, which could lead to different decisions depending on the assumed limits. The studies included in the analysis were generally at low risk of bias, and no downgrading was applied for this factor. Similarly, there was low concern about applicability in most studies, except for one that included only individuals with advanced HIV disease and another that included approximately 10% inpatients. No downgrading was applied for indirectness. The confidence intervals for sensitivity were narrow, with the lower limit being higher than the point estimate and lower limit of the WHO-recommended screen, and similar to the upper limit. This suggests that the confidence intervals would not likely lead to different decisions based on assumed credible limits. No downgrading was applied for imprecision in this case. Specificity estimates ranged from 90% to 96%, and no downgrading was applied for inconsistency. In studies evaluating molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests (mWRDs) versus the WHO-recommended 4-symptom screen followed by mWRD, sensitivity estimates ranged from 25% to 83% with overlapping confidence intervals. No downgrading was applied for inconsistency. Specificity estimates ranged from 90% to 96%, and no downgrading was applied for inconsistency. In summary, the diagnostic accuracy of various screening methods for tuberculosis in people living with HIV showed variability in sensitivity and specificity, with some studies demonstrating significant imprecision and inconsistency. These findings highlight the importance of considering the clinical context and population characteristics when interpreting diagnostic test results.
